title: Configuration management
blurb: Manage scope through configuration management: planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit.
question: On a new hospital wing, a contractor builds a wall from drawing version 2.1, not knowing that version 2.3 was approved a month earlier. Which process would have prevented this, and what are its five activities?

teach.h: Knowing exactly what you are building
teach.body: Configuration management is the set of administrative activities concerned with the creation, maintenance, controlled change and quality control of the scope of work. In plain English: every product, component and document that makes up the scope is identified, labelled and versioned, only authorised changes are made to it, and records always show which version is current. These controlled things are called CONFIGURATION ITEMS: drawings, specifications, code, plans, even the requirements themselves.

steps.sub: How items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited, and by whom

steps.label: Identification
steps.sub: Pick the items, label each with a reference and version; baseline

steps.label: Control
steps.sub: Only authorised changes are made; versions issued and withdrawn

steps.label:
Status
accounting
steps.sub: Record and report each item's current version, status and history

steps.label:
Verification
audit

teach.caption: Learn the order: Planning, Identification, Control, Status accounting, Verification audit.

teach.h: Northgate Hospital wing: each activity in action
head: Activity
What happens
rows: Configuration plan: drawings and specs under control, PMO keeps the register
Each drawing labelled, e.g. NG-ARCH-014 v2.3
New version issued only after approval; old copies withdrawn
Register shows v2.3 current, what changed and when
Built wall checked against v2.3; register checked against site
teach.caption: Had control and status accounting worked, the superseded v2.1 would have been withdrawn and the register would have shown v2.3 as current.

teach.body: Without configuration management, people build from out-of-date versions, changes slip in without approval, and nobody can say exactly what was delivered. With it, everyone works from the same current version, the impact of a proposed change can be assessed because you know what each item is and what it connects to, there is an audit trail of how the scope evolved, and handover gives operations accurate records of what they now own. It matters most where errors are costly or safety-critical.

teach.caption: They depend on each other: configuration records feed the impact assessment of a change request, and an approved change updates the configuration and its records.
Every item has a unique reference and a version number, so anyone can tell exactly which one they are holding.

teach.h: Configuration management in linear vs iterative life cycles

rows.label: Baselines
values: Set for each increment or release

teach.caption: Iterative teams change things constantly, so disciplined versioning matters even more: every release must be traceable to exactly what was in it.

teach.text: Exam traps: configuration management does not DECIDE whether a change goes ahead (that is change control); it controls and records WHAT the items are and which version is current. Don't swap the last two activities: STATUS ACCOUNTING records and reports status and history; VERIFICATION AUDIT checks the items match requirements and the records match reality. The order is Planning, Identification, Control, Status accounting, Verification audit.

teach.caption: Memory hook: 'Please Identify Current Specification Versions'.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Planning: decide what will be controlled, how, and who is responsible.
Identification: select configuration items, label them uniquely, version them and baseline them.
Control: make sure only authorised changes are made, linked to change control.
Status accounting: keep and report records of each item's current version and change history.
Verification audit: confirm items match their requirements and records, e.g. before handover.
Configuration management controls the products that make up the scope and their versions.
Five activities in order: Planning, Identification, Control, Status accounting, Verification audit.
Change control decides whether; configuration management records what and which version.
Benefits: right version used, impact assessment, audit trail, accurate handover records.
Linear: baselines at gates. Iterative: every release baselined and version-controlled.

summary: You can now explain how configuration management manages scope through planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit, and why each activity matters. You can also distinguish it from change control and describe how it works in linear and iterative life cycles.

A.q: Which is the correct order of the configuration management activities?
options: Identification, planning, control, verification audit, status accounting
Planning, control, identification, status accounting, verification audit
Planning, identification, control, status accounting, verification audit
Planning, identification, status accounting, control, verification audit
A.why: First plan the approach, then identify and label the items, control changes to them, record their status, and finally audit that items and records match.

whyNot.0: Planning comes first, and status accounting comes before the verification audit.
whyNot.1: You can't control items you haven't yet identified.
whyNot.3: Control comes before status accounting: changes are controlled, then their status is recorded.

options: A risk recorded on the project risk register
A product or document placed under control
A team member assigned to a work package
A change request waiting for a decision
A.why: A configuration item is any product, component or document (such as a drawing, specification or piece of code) that is identified, versioned and controlled.

whyNot.0: Risks are managed through risk management and the risk register.
whyNot.2: People are allocated through resource management, not configuration management.
whyNot.3: Change requests are handled by change control; they may affect configuration items but aren't items themselves.

A.q: Which configuration management activity decides how items will be identified, controlled, recorded and audited, and who is responsible?
options: Identification
Control
Status accounting
Planning
A.why: Planning sets out the whole approach: which items are controlled, how, with what tools and by whom.

whyNot.0: Identification applies the plan by selecting and labelling items.
whyNot.1: Control manages changes to items once they are identified.
whyNot.2: Status accounting records and reports each item's status and history.

B.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between change control and configuration management?
options: Change control decides if; CM records what changed
Change control is linear; CM is for iterative work
Change control logs versions; CM approves changes
Change control is for users; CM is for the sponsor
B.why: Change control decides WHETHER a change is made. Configuration management (CM) controls and records WHAT the items are and which version is current, so only authorised changes are implemented.

whyNot.1: Both are used in both life cycles.
whyNot.2: This swaps them: CM keeps versions, change control leads to the decision.
whyNot.3: Neither is defined by who uses it; both serve the whole project.

B.q: Before handover of a new hospital wing, a check finds the as-built drawings don't match the ventilation actually installed. Which activity has found this?
options: Identification
Verification audit
Status accounting
Planning
B.why: A verification audit checks that the items match their requirements and that the records match reality, which is exactly the mismatch found here.

whyNot.0: Identification labels and baselines items; it doesn't check them against reality.
whyNot.2: Status accounting keeps the records; the audit is what tests them against what is built.
whyNot.3: Planning sets the approach at the start; it doesn't inspect the built work.

B.q: Why is configuration management especially valuable at handover to operations?
options: It removes the need for acceptance testing
It lets the team skip the post-project review
Users get accurate records of what they own
It closes the change log automatically
B.why: Accurate, verified configuration records tell the operations team exactly what they have received, in which version, so they can run and maintain it.

whyNot.0: Acceptance testing is still needed to show the outputs meet their criteria.
whyNot.1: Reviews are still needed to capture lessons learned.
whyNot.3: The change log is closed by the team as part of closure, not by configuration management.

C.q: On a building project, superseded drawings were never withdrawn from site, and a team built from an old version. Which activity should have prevented this?
options: Planning
Identification
Control
Verification audit
C.why: Control makes sure only authorised changes are made and that the current version is issued while superseded versions are withdrawn.

whyNot.0: Planning should say how withdrawal works, but it is control that carries it out on site.
whyNot.1: The drawings were labelled with versions; the failure was in managing their issue and withdrawal.
whyNot.3: An audit might later detect the error, but it wouldn't prevent it.

C.q: A software team releases a new increment every month. How does configuration management typically work for it?
options: It isn't needed, as the backlog replaces it
It's done once, at the end of the project
It's handled only by the product owner
Each release is baselined and versioned
C.why: In iterative delivery each increment or release becomes a baseline, and version control records exactly what went into it, so releases are traceable and can be rolled back.

whyNot.0: The backlog holds requirements; it doesn't control versions of what was built.
whyNot.1: With monthly releases, leaving it to the end would lose track of what was delivered.
whyNot.2: It is a team and project discipline, not just one role's job.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of configuration management?
options: Deciding if a change should be approved
Knowing which version of each item is current
Supporting impact assessment of changes
Keeping an audit trail of how items evolved
C.why: Deciding whether to approve a change belongs to change control. Configuration management supplies the records that inform that decision.

whyNot.1: Knowing the current version is a core purpose of configuration management.
whyNot.2: Configuration records show what an item is and what it links to, which supports impact assessment.
whyNot.3: Status accounting builds exactly this audit trail.

reteach.title: Think of a band's setlist and music
reteach.question: A band is rehearsing for a music festival. The songs keep being rearranged. How do they make sure everyone plays the same version on the night?

blocks.body: The band leader decides how charts will be named and who keeps them (PLANNING). Each chart gets a title and version: 'Opener v4' (IDENTIFICATION). Only the leader can issue a new arrangement, and old copies are binned (CONTROL). A shared list shows the current version of every song and what changed (STATUS ACCOUNTING). At the final rehearsal, they check every player's folder matches the list, and the list matches what they actually play (VERIFICATION AUDIT).

blocks.text: Deciding to rearrange a song is a change decision (change control). Making sure everyone then has the new version, and only that version, is configuration management.

explain.body: Planning sets out what will be controlled, how and by whom. Identification then selects the configuration items, gives each a unique reference and version number, and sets the baseline: the agreed starting configuration.

test.q: During identification, what happens to each configuration item?
options: It is given a risk owner and a score
It is costed against a work package
It is checked against its requirements
It gets a unique reference and version
test.why: Identification labels each item uniquely with a reference and version so it can be tracked and controlled.

whyNot.0: Risk owners and scores belong to risk management.
whyNot.1: Costing against work packages is the CBS, not configuration identification.
whyNot.2: Checking items against requirements is the verification audit.

explain.body: Control makes sure that only authorised changes are made to configuration items. A new version is issued only once a change has been approved through change control, and superseded versions are withdrawn so nobody works from them.

test.q: Which statement best describes the CONTROL activity?
options: Only authorised changes are made to items
The current status of every item is reported
Items are checked against the records
Items are first selected and labelled
test.why: Control ensures items change only through authorised, approved changes, with versions properly issued and withdrawn.

whyNot.2: Checking items against records is the verification audit.
whyNot.3: Selecting and labelling items is identification.

explain.body: Status accounting records and reports the current status of every configuration item: its version, whether it is draft, approved or superseded, and the history of changes made to it. It answers 'what is current, and how did it get here?'

test.q: A sponsor asks: 'Which version of the specification are we building to, and what has changed since last month?' Which activity provides the answer?
options: Verification audit
Status accounting
Identification
Planning
test.why: Status accounting maintains and reports the current version and change history of each item.

whyNot.0: A verification audit checks items against requirements and records; it doesn't routinely report status.
whyNot.2: Identification labels the items; it doesn't track their changing status.
whyNot.3: Planning sets the approach; it doesn't hold the live records.

explain.body: A verification audit checks that the configuration items match their requirements and that the configuration records match what actually exists. It is often carried out before key decision points and before handover, so the project hands over exactly what the records say.

test.q: What does a configuration verification audit check?
options: That changes were approved by the sponsor
That risks have owners and agreed actions
That items match requirements and records
That benefits are realised after handover
test.why: The verification audit confirms the items meet their requirements and that the records accurately reflect them.

whyNot.0: Approval of changes is part of change control.
whyNot.1: Risk ownership is checked through risk management.
whyNot.3: Benefits realisation is tracked through benefits management, after the project.
